I don't really know about two weeks, or keeping track of time like that. I know they didn't. \n\nIt wasn't like they came out and said \"we don't want you,\" because they can't do that, right? They have rules. So they did it through the school portal. Every time they sent an email or left a comment on one of my assignments, they would change the wording just a tiny bit. Like, they wouldn't use standard phrasing. They would use these specific, little altered words, and I realized it was a code. They were marking me. They were using those little wording changes to flag me in the system as someone who shouldn't be allowed to work in healthcare. \n\nI tried to show my mom. I printed out all the emails and the assignment rubrics and I highlighted the words—like how one professor said \"ensure careful attention\" instead of just \"pay attention,\" or how the practicum coordinator kept using the word \"monitor\" in this really specific way. I laid them all out on the kitchen table to show her the pattern, how it was this whole coordinated thing between the professors and the clinic people to push me out. But she just sighed and told me they were just regular messages. She said I was reading too much into it and that professors just talk like that. But she doesn't get it. She doesn't understand that they have to do it that way so they don't get sued, but they still have to make sure the other people in the program know I'm marked. Even now that I'm not going to classes, I know the mark is still there in the portal. They made sure of it.\n\nDoctor: Have there been times when you believed the school was marking you even when you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: Well, I... I don't really think it works like that. It's not about being depressed. Because the emails were there before I stopped doing things, and they're still there now while I'm just sitting in my room. It's not like the mark in the portal goes away just because I'm sitting on the edge of my bed all day, you know? \n\nI remember when I first noticed it, I was actually doing okay. I was still knitting those scarves, I was still writing in my notebooks every night, using my different colored pens. I was going to my classes and getting my assignments done. I was just sitting at my desk, looking at my laptop, and I saw that first email from the practicum coordinator. The one where she used the word \"monitor.\" And I just knew. I knew right then what they were doing. It didn't matter how I was feeling, it was just right there on the screen in black and white. And then the next week, the professor used that phrase, \"ensure careful attention,\" and I started printing them all out. \n\nSo it's not... it's not a mood thing. It's not because I'm heavy and tired now. The school did what they did, and they coordinated the whole thing, and that's just a fact of what happened. I could be out walking around the neighborhood looking at the trees like I used to, and it wouldn't change the fact that they coded those messages to flag me in the system. The mark is just there. It doesn't care if I'm happy or sad or just staring at the wall.\n\nDoctor: When you talk, do other people ever tell you that your thoughts or speech are hard to follow or seem jumbled?\n\nPatient: No, no one says that. I mean, my mom doesn't say that, and she's the only one I really talk to anymore. When I talk to her, I'm just telling her what I need, like if I want a glass of water or if I need her to pick up a different kind of soap from the store because the one she bought last time had a weird smell that made my head hurt. I explain it to her very clearly. I tell her exactly what I mean, from the beginning of the thought to the end. I don't jump around or get confused. \n\nLike yesterday, I was trying to explain to her why I couldn't eat the sandwich she made, because the bread was cut diagonally instead of straight across, and I explained the whole reason, step by step, about how the diagonal cut makes the corners too sharp and it changes the way the bread feels when you hold it. I went through the whole explanation, and she understood me perfectly. She just sighed and made another one. She never says my words are jumbled. She might not agree with me, like about the emails from the school and the way they marked me, but she never says she can't follow what I'm saying. I use all the right words. I make sure I do. I think about the words before I say them, and I put them in a line, like beads on a string, just one after the other so they make a perfect sentence. So, no, nobody tells me I'm hard to follow. They just... they just don't want to listen sometimes. But that's different. That's not because my words are wrong.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a time when you felt so energized or unusually up that you needed much less sleep than usual?\n\nPatient: No, I... I don't think so. I don't get energized like that. It's actually the exact opposite, really. I don't have times where I feel \"up\" or like I don't need to sleep. Sleep is... well, I sleep a lot. Or I try to, anyway. I mean, I spend most of my time in my room now, like I said before. I'm usually just sitting on the edge of my bed, and my limbs feel so heavy, like they're filled with wet sand or lead or something. I don't have this... this bursting energy to go do things or run around. \n\nI usually go to bed at like 9:30 or 10 o'clock every night because there's just nothing else to do, and I turn off the main overhead light, but I always leave the little desk lamp on because it casts this softer shadow against the closet door, and I just pull the heavy quilt up and wait to fall asleep. It's just... I'm just heavy. Even when I was still doing my notebooks and knitting the scarves, I still slept normal hours. I've never had a time where my body just didn't want to sleep. I don't even know what that would feel like, to be honest. I just feel tired.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel sad or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: No, I do not think sad is the right word. I mean, sad is when... when you drop something you really like or when a dog dies in a movie, right? That is sad. You cry when you are sad. I do not cry. I have not cried in... I do not even know how long it has been since I actually shed a tear. I just sit there. \n\nLike I was saying before about my bed, I just sit on the edge of the mattress. It is just a physical weight, pulling me down into the mattress, making it hard to even walk to the kitchen to get the water my mom leaves out for me on the counter next to the sink. But it is not a sad weight. It is just a completely empty weight. So I do not think depressed is right at all. I am just here. I am just existing in the room.\n\nDoctor: Do things that used to feel enjoyable to you, like knitting or journaling, still feel enjoyable now?\n\nPatient: No, they don't. I mean, I don't even do them at all anymore, so I wouldn't know if they feel enjoyable, but just looking at them doesn't make me feel anything. I have this wicker basket in the corner of my room, right next to the closet door I was telling you about, and it's completely full of yarn. There's this really thick, chunky mustard-yellow yarn right on top that I bought specifically to make a winter scarf, and the knitting needles are just sticking right out of the center of the skein. Months, probably. I just look at the basket from the bed. It doesn't look fun. It just looks like an impossible amount of work. \n\nAnd it is the exact same thing with my journaling. I just stare at her, or I maybe mumble that I'm fine, because actually trying to form a real sentence about why I'm not doing anything is just too exhausting. Hopeless? I... I don't think hopeless is the right word. Hopeless implies that you were actually hoping for something in the first place, right? Like, to feel hopeless, you have to have some kind of picture in your head of how things are supposed to be, and then feel devastated when they aren't that way. Like back when I was planning out that blanket, I had all the stitch counts in my black composition notebooks, and I hoped it would turn out perfectly square. If I messed up a row, maybe I'd feel frustrated. But hopeless? No, I don't think I feel hopeless. 

Because to feel deeply hopeless, you have to actually feel something deep, and I just... I don't. I don't sit on my bed with the blue anchors and cry about the future. I don't cry at all. It's not a sad feeling. It's not this crushing despair where I'm wishing things were different. It's just... flat. It's just the stripes of light moving across the beige carpet, from the window with the cheap plastic blinds, over and over. Hopeless is too big of an emotion. It takes energy to be hopeless, I think. You have to care that things are bad to feel hopeless about them. 

I just watch the dust motes float in the air when the sun hits the room. The heavy silver laptop sits on the desk with the dented corner, and the dead strings of mustard-yellow yarn sit in the wicker basket, and I just exist in the middle of it. I don't look at my mom's glossy bird calendar and feel hopeless about tomorrow, because tomorrow is just going to be another day of the sun moving the shadows around the room. There's no hope, but there's no hopelessness either. It's just... nothing. So no, I wouldn't say I've had days where I felt deeply hopeless. I don't have big feelings like that anymore.

I don't sit there and mark off fourteen little squares on my mom's glossy bird calendar in the kitchen. \n\nSo if you're asking me to perfectly slice out a two-week chunk of time where I was absolutely sure about the practicum emails—you know, the ones with the weird italics and the double spaces on my heavy silver laptop—but I somehow wasn't feeling like a completely hollowed-out shell... I just can't do it. I can't separate them like that. It’s not like I have this neat little diary where I wrote down, oh, today the school is marking me, but I feel totally fine and I really want to knit with my mustard-yellow yarn. It doesn't work like that. \n\nThe laptop is sitting right there on the desk with the dented corner, and the wicker basket of dead yarn is on the floor, and I'm on the bed with the blue anchors, and it's all just... it's all just one big heavy thing that sits on top of me. I can't tell you if there were fourteen days of the emails happening without the emptiness happening too, because it's all just a blur of the exact same day repeating over and over. I really just don't know how to give you the exact timeline you're looking for.\n\nDoctor: Before you ever noticed the school emails seemed coded, had there already been a period when you no longer enjoyed things like knitting or journaling?\n\nPatient: I... I really, really don't know how else to explain this to you. You're asking me about 'before' again, before the emails, before the coding, before the italics and the double spaces. But I just... I don't have a 'before' that I can see clearly anymore. It's like trying to look through a window that's completely frosted over, you know? Like the grass outside my window in the mornings, just completely covered in this thick, white frost where you can't even tell what color the grass underneath is supposed to be. \n\nBefore I noticed the practicum emails on my heavy silver laptop... was I already not enjoying the knitting? Was the mustard-yellow yarn already just sitting there in the wicker basket, doing nothing? Were the black composition notebooks already shoved to the side on the desk with the dented corner? I don't know. I honestly don't know. Because when I try to think back, when I try to picture myself sitting on the bed with the blue anchors and actually wanting to knit, actually wanting to write down stitch counts... it feels like I'm trying to remember someone else's life. \n\nI don't know if the emptiness swallowed me up first, and then I started seeing what the school was doing, or if I saw what the school was doing and then the emptiness came. It's not like my mom's glossy bird calendar in the kitchen where you can just flip back a page and say, 'Oh, look, October 12th, stopped liking yarn. November 3rd, noticed the coded emails.' It doesn't work like that. It's all just mashed together in my head. The stripes of light through the cheap plastic blinds, the beige carpet, the dead yarn, the heavy laptop, the emails... it's all just one big, heavy, confusing mess, and I can't pick it apart for you. I just can't. I'm sorry, but I really just don't know the order of any of it.\n\nDoctor: Have there been days when you felt deeply hopeless?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? I... I don't think hopeless is the right word. Hopeless implies that you were actually hoping for something in the first place, right? I don't sit on my bed with the blue anchors and cry about the future. I don't cry at all. It's not a sad feeling. It's not this crushing despair where I'm wishing things were different. It's just... flat. It's just the stripes of light moving across the beige carpet, from the window with the cheap plastic blinds, over and over. Hopeless is too big of an emotion. There's no hope, but there's no hopelessness either. It's just... nothing. So no, I wouldn't say I've had days where I felt deeply hopeless. I don't have big feelings like that anymore.\n\nDoctor: For at least two weeks, have you had the belief that the school was marking you during a time when you were not feeling this empty and unable to enjoy things?\n\nPatient: I... But she's always in there, and she makes the meals. She'll bring a plate into my room, or she'll call me out to the table, and I just eat it. Like yesterday, she made this chicken soup with those tiny, star-shaped noodles. I just sat at the table and watched the metal spoon go into the bowl, and then into my mouth, and then back into the bowl. Over and over. It's just a mechanical thing, you know? She's always hovering around, asking if I want a turkey sandwich, asking if I want a glass of orange juice. I chew the bread, and it's just texture in my mouth. It doesn't taste good, it doesn't taste bad, it's just... matter. Like back when I was planning out that blanket, I had all the stitch counts in my black composition notebooks, and I hoped it would turn out perfectly square. It takes energy to be hopeless, I think. You have to care that things are bad to feel hopeless about them. \n\nI just watch the dust motes float in the air when the sun hits the room. I don't look at my mom's glossy bird calendar and feel hopeless about tomorrow, because tomorrow is just going to be another day of the sun moving the shadows around the room.
